deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no mathematics: no derivation, formula or computation. It is a single English quotation copied out by Riemann, followed by a source reference.

Text: Newton says „That gravity should be innate, inherent, and essential to matter, so that one body may act upon another at a distance through a vacuum, without the mediation of anything else, by and through which their action and force may be conveyed from one to another, is to me so great an absurdity, that I believe no man who has in philosophical matters a competent faculty of thinking can ever fall into it.“ See the third letter to Bentley.

Source: Newton's third letter to Richard Bentley, dated 25 February 1692/3. It was first printed in 'Four Letters from Sir Isaac Newton to Doctor Bentley' (London, 1756). Riemann's copy matches the standard printed text almost word for word. He omits the sentence that follows in the original: 'Gravity must be caused by an Agent acting constantly according to certain Laws; but whether this Agent be material or immaterial, I have left to the Consideration of my Readers.' The next folio is a second, nearly identical copy of the same passage, possibly a fair copy or a draft.

Purpose (contextual, my inference): the bundle is 'Naturphilosophie'. Riemann rejected instantaneous action at a distance. He sought to explain gravitation, light and electricity through a continuous space-filling medium ('Stoff') that propagates action from point to point. Examples are his 1858 note on electrodynamics with retarded potentials and the fragments 'Gravitation und Licht' and 'Neue mathematische Principien der Naturphilosophie'. Newton's own rejection of unmediated action at a distance is the classic authority for such a programme, which is presumably why Riemann copied it, likely to cite in an essay or lecture.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics.

The quotation and the attribution to the third letter to Bentley are both accurate. The famous 'absurdity' passage is indeed in the third letter of 25 Feb 1692/3. Minor differences in punctuation and capitalisation from the 1756 print are immaterial.

results.what: Quotation of Newton's rejection of unmediated action at a distance, used as support for a field or medium theory of gravitation.
results.modern_name: Newton's letter to Bentley (critique of action at a distance); motivation for contact-action and field theories of gravity
results.usually_credited_to: Isaac Newton (1692/3). The quote is widely invoked by 19th-century field theorists such as Faraday and Maxwell.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a copied, well-known quotation from Newton with no original mathematical content. It is entirely expected given Riemann's documented opposition to action at a distance and his ether and medium programme in his natural-philosophy fragments. Interest is at most archival: it confirms that Riemann read the Bentley correspondence.
transcription_corrections: The machine transcription is essentially correct.
'Riemann 18' at the top is a later archival pencil annotation, not Riemann's hand. '(96)' is the circled archival folio number.
The 'p' in 'philosophical' resembles 'philozophical' in the handwriting, but 'philosophical' is clearly intended.
The opening quotation mark is the German low form („) and the closing mark is a high double mark. The transcription reflects this adequately.
